# Cellranger

In the course we are using single-cell RNAseq data generated using Chromium platform from 10X Genomics. After sequencing is done, count data is generated using 10X's Cellranger software. Cellranger has two commonly used workflows `count` and `aggr`. The `count` workflow is used to generate sample-wise gene count results whereas `aggr` is used to normalize (by sequencing depth) the count data and generate aggregated gene counts from multiple samples. Output directory structure between `count` and `aggr` pipelines differs slightly.

# Set output directories

In the following code block creates output directories for storing files and plots in a logical structure.

```{r create-directories}
out.dir        <- file.path("results")
res.dir        <- file.path(out.dir, "sc-rnaseq")
robj.dir       <- file.path(res.dir,"robj")
plot.dir       <- file.path(res.dir,"plots")
files.dir      <- file.path(res.dir,"files")
plot.data.dir  <- file.path(res.dir,"plots-data")
  
  ## create dirs
  dirs <- c(res.dir, robj.dir, plot.dir, files.dir, plot.data.dir)
  
  for(dir in dirs){
    dir.create(dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
  }
  
```

### Data format

Cellranger produces count data in sparse format which consists of 3 files. For sparse matrix manipulation (eg. import, export) in R please refer to `Matrix` library and its functions. 

* barcodes.tsv.gz
* features.tsv.gz
* matrix.mtx.gz

#### Cellbarcodes

The file `barcodes.tsv.gz` contains cell barcodes.

> NOTE: Following is a bash code. Ignore the error "gzip: stdout: Broken pipe"

```{bash barcodes, echo=FALSE}
DATA_DIR="/home/rstudio/abptds/data/sc-rnaseq/count"
SAMPLE="AML1_D"

echo "HEAD:"
zcat $DATA_DIR/$SAMPLE/barcodes.tsv.gz | head -n 4

echo -e "\nTAIL:"
zcat $DATA_DIR/$SAMPLE/barcodes.tsv.gz | tail -n 4

## check running numbers
echo -e "\nsample IDs"
zcat $DATA_DIR/$SAMPLE/barcodes.tsv.gz | cut -d "-" -f2 | sort | uniq
```

#### Features

The file `features.tsv.gz` contains feature names (in our case gene names in first and second column) and data type (in third column). 

> NOTE: Following is a bash code.

```{bash features}
SAMPLE="AML1_D"

DATA_DIR="/home/rstudio/abptds/data/sc-rnaseq/count"
zcat $DATA_DIR/$SAMPLE/features.tsv.gz | head
```

#### Data matrix

The file `matrix.mtx.gz` contains row position, column position and gene count for each gene. It contains non-zero counts.

> NOTE: Following is a bash code.


```{bash matrix}
SAMPLE="AML1_D"

DATA_DIR="/home/rstudio/abptds/data/sc-rnaseq/count"
zcat $DATA_DIR/$SAMPLE/matrix.mtx.gz | head
```


```{r count-data-loading, warning=FALSE}
suppressMessages(library(Seurat))
suppressMessages(library(gridExtra))
suppressMessages(library(ggplot2))
suppressMessages(library(glmGamPoi))


#############
data.dir <- "/home/rstudio/abptds/data/sc-rnaseq"

## data location of each sample
aml1.d.data <- Read10X(data.dir = file.path(data.dir, "count", "AML1_D"))
aml2.r.data <- Read10X(data.dir = file.path(data.dir, "count", "AML2_R"))
aml3.d.data <- Read10X(data.dir = file.path(data.dir, "count", "AML3_D"))
aml3.r.data <- Read10X(data.dir = file.path(data.dir, "count", "AML3_R"))

## create Seurat object of each samples
## It subsets original matrix if non-zeros values are provided to min.cells and  min.features
## min.cells   : Include features detected in at least this many cells
## min.features: Include cells where at least this many features are detected.
aml1.d <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = aml1.d.data, project = "AML1_D", min.cells = 5, min.features = 200)
aml2.r <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = aml2.r.data, project = "AML2_R", min.cells = 5, min.features = 200)
aml3.d <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = aml3.d.data, project = "AML3_D", min.cells = 5, min.features = 200)
aml3.r <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = aml3.r.data, project = "AML3_R", min.cells = 5, min.features = 200)

## remove intermediate objects and perform garbage collection

rm(aml2.r.data)
rm(aml3.d.data)
rm(aml3.r.data)
gc()

## Number of cells
cat( "\n",
     "AML1_D: ", length(Cells(aml1.d)),"\n",
     "AML2_R: ", length(Cells(aml2.r)),"\n",
     "AML3_D: ", length(Cells(aml3.d)),"\n",
     "AMl3_R: ", length(Cells(aml3.r)),"\n")
```


### MT Genes

Non-viable cells tend to have high mitochondrial gene expression. In this sub-section we calculate percentage of mitochondrial gene expressed in each cell. This will help us to filter non-viable cells out from our data. It is good to check mitochondrial gene names in your data because it differs from organism/annotation. Three starting letter of mitochondrial genes can be `MT-`, `Mt-` or `mt-`.

```{r mt-genes}
## check MT genes
all.genes <- rownames(aml1.d)
all.genes[grep("^MT-", all.genes)]

## calculate MT % for each samples separately
aml1.d[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(aml1.d, pattern = "^MT-")
aml2.r[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(aml2.r, pattern = "^MT-")
aml3.d[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(aml3.d, pattern = "^MT-")
aml3.r[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(aml3.r, pattern = "^MT-")

```

### QC Plots

In single cell expression data, commonly used quality matrices are:

* Number of total gene count per cell (`nFeature`).
* Number of unique gene count (UMI or unique molecular identifier) per cell (`nCount`).
* Percentage of mitochondrial expressed.

In the following code block we all three matrices in violin plots.

```{r QC-vln-plot}
vp1 <- VlnPlot(aml1.d, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"), ncol = 3, cols = "#999999")
vp2 <- VlnPlot(aml2.r, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"), ncol = 3, cols = "#E69F00")
vp3 <- VlnPlot(aml3.d, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"), ncol = 3, cols = "#56B4E9")
vp4 <- VlnPlot(aml3.r, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"), ncol = 3, cols = "#FF9999")

vp1; vp2; vp3; vp4
```

In the following code block we visualize `nCount_RNA` versus `percent.mt` and `nCount_RNA` versus `nFeature_RNA`.

```{r QC-scatter-plots}

sc1 <- FeatureScatter(aml1.d, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "percent.mt", cols = "#999999") + 
         FeatureScatter(aml1.d, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "nFeature_RNA", cols = "#999999")

sc2 <- FeatureScatter(aml2.r, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "percent.mt", cols = "#E69F00") + 
         FeatureScatter(aml2.r, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "nFeature_RNA", cols = "#E69F00")

sc3 <- FeatureScatter(aml3.d, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "percent.mt", cols = "#56B4E9") + 
         FeatureScatter(aml3.d, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "nFeature_RNA", cols = "#56B4E9")

sc4 <- FeatureScatter(aml3.r, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "percent.mt", cols = "#FF9999") + 
           theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust=1)) +
       FeatureScatter(aml3.r, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "nFeature_RNA", cols = "#FF9999") +
           theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust=1))



sc1; sc2; sc3; sc4;
```

### QC plots using Ggplot

Generating plots outside of Seurat package gives more flexibility and customization. However, to make custom plots, you should be able to find right data from  from a Seurat object's slot. Here we use `ggplots` to generate similar plots. In Seurat meta-data is stored in a slot `seuratObj@meta.data`. 

```{r QC-ggplot}
## Lets have a look into Seurat meta-data
head(aml1.d@meta.data)

## using ggplot
ggplot(aml1.d@meta.data, aes(x=nCount_RNA, y=nFeature_RNA)) + 
  geom_point(color="#FF9999")
```

### Top expressed genes

It is often a good idea to check list of top expressed genes. Here we check only for samples `AML1_D`. 

> First three lines of codes in the following code block is from NBIS Sweden.

```{r top-exp-genes}
C = aml1.d@assays$RNA@layers$counts
rownames(C) <- rownames( aml1.d@assays$RNA )
C@x = C@x/rep.int(colSums(C), diff(C@p))
most_expressed <- order(Matrix::rowSums(C), decreasing = T)[20:1]

a <- t(as.matrix(C[most_expressed, ]))
dat <- stack(as.data.frame(a))
colnames(dat) <- c("Percentage", "Gene")

ggplot(dat) + 
	geom_boxplot(aes(x = Gene, y = Percentage, color=Gene)) +
	coord_flip() +
	labs(y = "% total count per cell") +
	theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Filtering

Rationale behind filtering:
* Low-quality/empty cells have very low gene count.
* Doublets have very high gene count.


#### Manual filtering
Here we filter every sample separately.

```{r filtering-sep-data}

aml1.d.filt <- subset(aml1.d, subset = nFeature_RNA > 500 & nFeature_RNA < 3500 & percent.mt < 10)
aml2.r.filt <- subset(aml2.r, subset = nFeature_RNA > 500 & nFeature_RNA < 3000 & percent.mt < 10)
aml3.d.filt <- subset(aml3.d, subset = nFeature_RNA > 500 & nFeature_RNA < 2500 & percent.mt < 10)
aml3.r.filt <- subset(aml3.r, subset = nFeature_RNA > 500 & nFeature_RNA < 3000 & percent.mt < 10)

## 
aml1.d.raw <- aml1.d

## remove objects
## aml1.d will be used in exercise 1
#rm(aml1.d)
rm(aml2.r)
rm(aml3.d)
rm(aml3.r)
gc()

## Plots of filtered data
vp1 <- VlnPlot(aml1.d.filt, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"), ncol = 3, cols = "#999999")
vp2 <- VlnPlot(aml2.r.filt, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"), ncol = 3, cols = "#E69F00")
vp3 <- VlnPlot(aml3.d.filt, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"), ncol = 3, cols = "#56B4E9")
vp4 <- VlnPlot(aml3.r.filt, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"), ncol = 3, cols = "#FF9999")

vp1; vp2; vp3; vp4

```

#### Advance filtering

This is an optional section. Thus, it is recommended to run if time permits.

There are many methods for detecting doublets from single cell data. In the following code block we use *scDblFinder* R package for automatic doublet detection.

Please refer to doublet detection tools from [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cels.2020.11.008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cels.2020.11.008).

```{r advanced-fitlering}
suppressMessages(library(scDblFinder))

temp.sce <- as.SingleCellExperiment(aml1.d, assay="RNA")

## For 10x data, it is usually safe to leave the dbr empty, and it will be automatically estimated.
temp.sce <- scDblFinder(temp.sce)

plot.data <- as.data.frame(temp.sce@colData)


ggplot(plot.data, aes(x=nCount_RNA, y=nFeature_RNA, col=scDblFinder.class)) + geom_point()


## violin plot

## Convert data into tidy format
plot.data.tidy <- reshape2::melt(plot.data[,c("scDblFinder.class", "nFeature_RNA")])


## violin plot
p1 <- ggplot(plot.data.tidy , aes(x=variable, y=value)) +  
  geom_jitter(alpha=0.6, aes(color=scDblFinder.class))+
  geom_violin(alpha=0.0)

p2 <- ggplot(plot.data, aes(x=nCount_RNA, y=nFeature_RNA, color=scDblFinder.class)) + 
         geom_point() +
         theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust=1))

p1+p2


## remove doublets from Seurat obejct
singlets <- rownames(plot.data[plot.data$scDblFinder.class=="singlet",])

aml.d.sing <- subset(aml1.d, cells=singlets)

## remove objects
rm(temp.sce)
rm(plot.data)
rm(plot.data.tidy)
rm(singlets)
rm(aml.d.sing)
```


### Normalization

Sequencing reaction happens in each cell independent of others cells. This creates differences in gene count distribution. To make gene expression distributions comparable, we have to normalize gene expression of each cell. 


Lets normalize each samples separately first. Since non-aggregated data is not normalized by sequencing depth, it is recommended to use SCTransform normalization method to account for the sequencing depth bias. In the following code we have used `vars.to.regress` to regress-out effect coming from mitochondrial gene expression. Removal of unnecessary variation will be discussed in session 2.

```{r SCTransform}

aml1.d <- SCTransform(aml1.d.filt, vars.to.regress = "percent.mt", variable.features.n = 500, verbose = FALSE)
aml2.r <- SCTransform(aml2.r.filt, vars.to.regress = "percent.mt", variable.features.n = 500, verbose = FALSE)
aml3.d <- SCTransform(aml3.d.filt, vars.to.regress = "percent.mt", variable.features.n = 500, verbose = FALSE)
aml3.r <- SCTransform(aml3.r.filt, vars.to.regress = "percent.mt", variable.features.n = 500, verbose = FALSE)

## We rename "-1" part of the barcode
## aml1.d : "-1" ( "-1" is already there. Thus, no need to do anything)
## aml2.r : "-2"
## aml3.d : "-3"
## aml3.r " "-4"
aml2.r <- RenameCells(aml2.r, new.names = gsub("\\-1", "\\-2", Cells(aml2.r)))
aml3.d <- RenameCells(aml3.d, new.names = gsub("\\-1", "\\-3", Cells(aml3.d)))
aml3.r <- RenameCells(aml3.r, new.names = gsub("\\-1", "\\-4", Cells(aml3.r)))

## Combine the data and remove intermediate objects
aml <- merge(aml1.d,  list(aml2.r, aml3.d, aml3.r))

## check cell number per samples
head(aml@meta.data)
tail(aml@meta.data)
## remove intermediate objects
rm(aml1.d.filt)
rm(aml2.r.filt)
rm(aml3.d.filt)
rm(aml3.r.filt)

gc()
```




## Using aggregated count data

The directory `data/sc-rnaseq/aggregate` contains combined (normalized by sequencing depth) count data. 

Following is the directory structure generated using Cellranger `aggr` workflow. Count data (output from Cellranger `count`) from all the samples were used as inputs. In this course we use data from `filtered_gene_bc_matrices_mex` directory. The file `aggregation_csv.csv` contains samples being used in the analysis. In the aggregated data cell barcodes have running number `-1`, `-2` , `-3` and `-4` as a prefix. These running numbers are sample identifiers corresponding to the sample order in the file `aggregation_csv.csv`.

### Data format

The aggregate data format is similar to the coutn data format containing the following files. The aggrete data contains data from two or moe samples.

* barcodes.tsv.gz
* features.tsv.gz
* matrix.mtx.gz

> NOTE: Following is a bash code.

```{bash}
DATA_DIR="data/sc-rnaseq/aggregate"

zcat $DATA_DIR/barcodes.tsv.gz | head

zcat $DATA_DIR/barcodes.tsv.gz | tail
```


> NOTE: Following is a bash code.

```{bash}
DATA_DIR="data/sc-rnaseq/aggregate"

zcat $DATA_DIR/features.tsv.gz | head

```

```{bash}
DATA_DIR="data/sc-rnaseq/aggregate"

zcat $DATA_DIR/matrix.mtx.gz | head
```

Now, we import the aggregate count data in the following code block.

```{r agg-data-loading}

## load aggregate data [readily sequencing depth normalized]
aml <- Read10X(data.dir = file.path(data.dir, "aggregate"))
aml.all <- CreateSeuratObject(counts=aml, names.delim = "-", names.field = 2)

## get current identities
levels(aml.all)
table( Idents(aml.all) )

## set new identities
aml.all <- RenameIdents(aml.all, '1' = "AML2_R", "2" = "AML1_D", "3"="AML3_D", "4"="AML3_R")
table( Idents(aml.all) )

## add 'sample' column to aml@meta.data dataframe
aml.all <- AddMetaData(aml.all, Idents(aml.all), col.name = "sample")

## number of cells
table(aml.all@meta.data$sample)


```


> **Question:** Find out why we have used the arguments`names.delim` and `names.field` in the function `CreateSeuratObject`.


### MT genes

With the aggregate data, we can calculate mitochondrial gene percentage using just one-liner syntax.

```{r mt-genes-aggr}
aml.all[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(aml.all, pattern = "^MT-")
```

### QC plots

In the following code block QC plots contain all the samples. Thus, with aggregated data it is easier to create plots with fewer line of code.

```{r QC-vln-plot-aggr}
vp5 <- VlnPlot(aml.all, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"))
vp5


sc5 <- FeatureScatter(aml.all, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "percent.mt") +
           theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust=1)) +
       FeatureScatter(aml.all, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "nFeature_RNA") +
           theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust=1))

sc5

```
### Filtering

When it comes to aggregated data, we have to use different filtering threshold for each sample. Thus, The filtering on aggregated data results splitting of the data. We have to merge the splits afterwards.

```{r filtering-agg-data}
## Filter
temp1 <- subset(aml.all, subset = nFeature_RNA > 500 & nFeature_RNA < 3500 & percent.mt < 10 & sample=="AML1_D")
temp2 <- subset(aml.all, subset = nFeature_RNA > 500 & nFeature_RNA < 3000 & percent.mt < 10 & sample=="AML2_R")
temp3 <- subset(aml.all, subset = nFeature_RNA > 500 & nFeature_RNA < 2500 & percent.mt < 10 & sample=="AML3_D")
temp4 <- subset(aml.all, subset = nFeature_RNA > 500 & nFeature_RNA < 3000 & percent.mt < 10 & sample=="AML3_R")

## create a new aggregated data object
aml.filt <- merge(temp1,  list(temp2, temp3, temp4))


## plot
VlnPlot(aml.filt, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"))


## ggplot filtering plots
nfeat.tidy <- reshape2::melt(aml.all@meta.data[,c("nFeature_RNA","sample")], measure.vars=c("nFeature_RNA")) 

ggplot(nfeat.tidy, aes(x=value, fill=sample, colour=sample) ) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.1) 


## plot with filtering threshold
ggplot(nfeat.tidy[nfeat.tidy$sample=="AML3_R",], aes(x=value, fill=sample, colour=sample) ) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 500, linetype=2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3000, linetype=2)

## remove temp objects and run garbage collector
rm(temp1)
rm(temp2)
rm(temp3)
rm(temp4)
gc()

```
### Normalization

For aggregated data is it not essential to use SCTransform normalization because aggregated data is sequencing depth normalized data. Thus, we normalize the raw count data using Seurat's default method `LogNormalize`. LogNormalize divides count of a cell by its total count and multiplies by `scale.factor` (default: 10000). The result is then log transferred using `log1p` which computes natural logarithm of the given value plus one. This is done to avoid getting `-Inf` values while using `log`.


```{r normalization, message=FALSE}
aml.filt <- NormalizeData(aml.filt)
```

Finally, we have completed the data loading, QC and the normalization step. In the following code block we save the final object `aml` into a file.

```{r save-final-object}
aml <- JoinLayers(aml.filt)

saveRDS(aml, file = file.path(robj.dir,"aml.RDS"))

rm(list = ls())
gc()
```

After saving the object, clear the environment variable by pressing 🧹 ("Environment"  tab on the top right).

# Feature Selection, Removal of Undesired Sources of Variation, and Dimensionality Reduction

In this section, we will focus on feature selection, removal of undesired sources of variation and dimensionality reduction. Before processing we have to load the object saved in the previous section.

Participants are expected to watch lecture videos of the following modules from [https://uppsala.instructure.com/courses/52011/modules](https://uppsala.instructure.com/courses/52011/modules).

- Dimensionality Reduction
- Data Integration

## Identifying Highly Variable Genes

Highly variable genes (HVGs) are genes that show the most variation across cells (i.e., they are highly expressed in some cells and lowly expressed in others). There are two main reasons to identify highly variable genes (HVGs):

- To reduce the dimensionality of the data (curse of dimensionality) and
- To identify genes that are driving the biological variation in the data.

```{r highly-variable-genes, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
suppressMessages(library(Seurat))
suppressMessages(library(gridExtra))
suppressMessages(library(ggplot2))
suppressMessages(library(glmGamPoi))


## Load the saved object from previous session
aml <- readRDS("results/sc-rnaseq/robj/aml.RDS")

## calculate variable features
aml <- FindVariableFeatures(aml, nfeatures=2000, verbose = FALSE)


## Get top 10 most highly variable genes
top10 <- head(VariableFeatures(aml), 10)
top10

## Plot HVGs with labels
hvg <- VariableFeaturePlot(aml) + labs(title = 'HVGs')
hvg.labelled <- LabelPoints(plot = hvg, points = top10, repel = TRUE) + labs(title = 'HVGs, top10 HVGs labeled')

hvg.labelled

```

## Removal of undesired sources of variation (1/2)
Removing unwanted sources of variation helps find the biological sources of variation we are actually interested in. Here, we will regressing-out mitochondrial RNA content and cell cycle effects, which are common sources of variation in single-cell RNA-seq data. For the sake of this tutorial, we will regressing-out only the mitochondrial RNA content, and then perform dimensionality reduction and visualization.

Furthermore, we will regress-out cell cycle effects and perform dimensionality reduction and visualization again to see how it affects the data.

In practice, it makes sense to go back to this step also after clustering and visualization, as the clustering results can help identify unwanted sources of variation that were not apparent before, or reveal that some sources of variation that were removed were actually biologically relevant.

```{r mt-regress-out}
## Save the object before regressing out confounders
aml.before.regression <- aml

## Regress out mitochondrial content and scale data
aml.mtregressed <- ScaleData(aml.before.regression, vars.to.regress = "percent.mt", verbose = FALSE)

```


## Dimensionality Reduction
Humans are usually not good at grasping contexts, especially in more than three dimensions. Dimensionality reduction techniques help us visualize the data in 2D or 3D, while retaining most of the variation in the data.


### Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA is the most common dimensionality reduction technique. It helps in visualizing the data and identifying clusters, and the resulting principal components (expressing most of the variation in our dataset) can be used in downstream analyses, such as embedding the data in lower dimensions in UMAP or t-SNE.


```{r}
## perform PCA
aml.mtregressed <- RunPCA(aml.mtregressed,
                          features = VariableFeatures(object = aml.mtregressed),
                          ndims.print = 1:3,
                          nfeatures.print = 5)


## Visualize top genes associated with the first 2 PCA components
VizDimLoadings(aml.mtregressed,
                          dims = 1:3,
                          reduction = "pca",
                          ncol = 3)


## Plot dimensionality reduction on two dimensions as a scatter plot
DimPlot(aml.mtregressed, reduction = "pca") + 
  labs(title = 'PCA')

# Plot heatmaps for top genes and cells associated with the first two principal components
DimHeatmap(aml.mtregressed,
                      dims = 1:6,
                      cells = 500,
                      balanced = TRUE,
                      fast = FALSE)

## Elbow plot
ElbowPlot(aml.mtregressed, ndims = 50)
```

How do the results differ before and after regressing out mitochondrial RNA?

> Visit the following website to get a better feeling for PCA: https://setosa.io/ev/principal-component-analysis/


## Removal of undesired sources of variation (2/2)

Cell cycle is a major source of variation in single-cell RNA-seq data. Correcting for cell cycle effects helps in identifying the biological sources of variation we are interested in.


```{r cell-cycle-genes}
# Load cell cycle genes
cc.genes <- Seurat::cc.genes.updated.2019

cat("S-Phase genes:\n", paste(cc.genes$s.genes, sep=""), "\n\n")
cat("G2M-Phase genes:\n", paste(cc.genes$g2m.genes, sep=""), "\n")

```

Lets perform the cell cycle scoring in the original `aml` object for later use.

```{r cell-cycle-scoring}
# Score cell cycle phase
aml <- CellCycleScoring(aml,
                        s.features = cc.genes$s.genes,
                        g2m.features = cc.genes$g2m.genes,
                        set.ident = TRUE,
                        layer = "data")

# Visualize the distribution of a few of the cell cycle markers, top row being S phase and bottom row being G2M phase genes
RidgePlot(aml, features = c("NUSAP1", "PCNA"), ncol = 2)
```

Plot (using signal only from the cell cycle genes) PCA before regressing-out cell cycle effects.

```{r}
## copy the object
aml.before.cc.regression <- aml

## Scale data without regressing-out cell cycle genes
aml.before.cc.regression <- ScaleData(aml.before.cc.regression,
                                       features = VariableFeatures(aml.before.cc.regression),
                                       layer = "data"
)

## Run PCA on cell cycle genes only to see if cells separate by cell cycle phase
aml.before.cc.regression <- RunPCA(aml.before.cc.regression,
                                    features = c(cc.genes$s.genes, cc.genes$g2m.genes) )

# Visualize PCA results
DimPlot(aml.before.cc.regression,
        reduction = "pca",
        group.by = "Phase")


## remove object
rm(aml.before.cc.regression)
gc()

```

Plot PCA after regressing-out cell cycle effects.

```{r}
aml.after.cc.regression <- aml

## Scale data by regressing out cell cycle signal
aml.after.cc.regression <- ScaleData(aml.after.cc.regression,
                                     features = VariableFeatures(aml.after.cc.regression),
                                     layer = "data",
                                     vars.to.regress = c("S.Score", "G2M.Score"),
                                     verbose = FALSE)

## Run PCA on cell cycle genes only to see if cells separate by cell cycle phase
aml.after.cc.regression <- RunPCA(aml.after.cc.regression,
                                    features = c(cc.genes$s.genes, cc.genes$g2m.genes) )

## Visualize PCA
DimPlot(aml.after.cc.regression,
        reduction = "pca",
        group.by = "Phase",
        alpha = 0.3)


## remove object
rm(aml.after.cc.regression)
gc()
```

## Exercise 5

In some cases, regressing out all variation associated with cell cycle can be detrimental for downstream analyses, particularly in differentiating processes (like murine hematopoiesis), where differentiated cells are proliferating (or vice versa). In such cases, regressing out all cell cycle effects can blur the distinction between stem and progenitor cells as well. Thus, here we are only regressing out the difference between the S and G2M phase scores (S-Score - G2M-Score), so that signals separating non-cycling cells and cycling cells will be maintained, but differences in cell cycle phase among proliferating cells (which are often uninteresting), will be regressed out.

Make a copy of the object `aml` and store it as `temp`, then perform the following on that object:

- Calculate the difference between S and G2M scores. Hint: they are stored in the columns S.Score and G2M.Score of the object.
- Regress out the difference between S and G2M scores using the `vars.to.regress` parameter in `ScaleData()`.
- Run PCA on the regressed object and visualize the results. How do the results differ from regressing out all cell cycle effects?


## Regress out confounders all together

Why? If you regress out confounders one at a time in separate ScaleData calls, the residuals from each step become the input for the next, meaning you are regressing against an already transformed dataset. This can lead to unintended interactions between regressors and less interpretable results. Similarly, if factors are regressed out sequentially, each round of regression could introduce artifacts or distortions in the variance structure of the data, particularly if the factors are correlated. Thus, it is recommended to regress out all confounders together.

Here, we found both mitochondrial RNA content and cell cycle effects to be confounders. We will regress them out together and visualize the results.

```{r regress-out-all}
## Scale data by regressing-out percent.mt, S.Score and G2M.Score
aml <- ScaleData(aml,
                 vars.to.regress = c("percent.mt", "S.Score", "G2M.Score"),
                 layer = "data",
                 verbose = FALSE)


## Run PCA
aml <- RunPCA(aml,
              features = VariableFeatures(aml),
              ndims.print = 1:3,
              nfeatures.print = 20)


## Visualize PCA results
DimPlot(aml,
        reduction = "pca",
        group.by = "Phase") + 
  ggtitle("PCA After Regression, Grouped by Phase")


## Visualize top genes associated with the first 2 PCA components
VizDimLoadings(aml,
               dims = 1:2,
               reduction = "pca") + 
  ggtitle("Top Genes PCA Loadings After Regression")

```


## Data Integration / Batch Correction

### Sample Integration

This step is optional and should only be performed when you suspect large differences between samples (e.g., different batches, different sequencing runs, etc.), or when you want to integrate multiple datasets from different sources (e.g. different chemistry, facilities, etc.). In this case, our data was generated using the same chemistry and facility, and the samples look fairly mixed in the PCA and embeddings, so we will not perform integration here, but we will show you how it works, and you can try how it affects the PCA and clustering results, if time permits. There are many methods available for data integration, such as CCA, MNN, Harmony, scVI, Limma, Liger, and many more. Here, we will use the `FindIntegrationAnchors` and `IntegrateData` functions in Seurat, which represents an anchor-based (RPCA-based) integration method.

```{r}
options(future.globals.maxSize = 2 * 1024^3)

temp <- aml

## Split the object by sample
temp.list <- SplitObject(temp, split.by = "sample")

## Identify variable features for each dataset independently, selecting the top 10% most variable genes as highly variable genes
temp.list <- lapply(X = temp.list, FUN = function(x) {
  x <- FindVariableFeatures(x, selection.method = "vst", nfeatures = 0.1 * nrow(x[["RNA"]]), layer = "data")
})


##  Select genes that are useful for comparing datasets.
## * Seurat examines the variable features in each dataset.
## * It prioritizes genes that are variable across datasets.
## * It returns a list of 2,000 genes to use for integration.
anchor.features <- SelectIntegrationFeatures(object.list = temp.list)



temp.list <- lapply(X = temp.list, FUN = function(x) {
  x <- ScaleData(x, features = anchor.features, verbose = FALSE)
  x <- RunPCA(x, features = anchor.features, verbose = FALSE)
})

## Find pairs of cells that appear biologically similar across datasets.
temp.anchors <- FindIntegrationAnchors(object.list = temp.list, 
                                       anchor.features = anchor.features, 
                                       reduction = "rpca",
                                       verbose = FALSE)

## Use the anchors to correct differences between datasets.
temp.combined <- IntegrateData(anchorset = temp.anchors, verbose = FALSE)

# The integrated data is stored in a separate assay named 'integrated'
print(temp.combined@assays)


print(colnames(temp.combined[[]]))
```

Now, our integrated data is stored in the integrated assay. As you can see, this assay does not contain a data or counts layer anymore, which means that our data is now represented in the latent space, and we don’t have access to a count matrix anymore. The latent space is a lower-dimensional representation of the data that captures shared structure across cells, where items resembling each other are closer together and items that are dissimilar are further apart. You can think of it as being similar to the PCA space, but it is learned from the data and is not directly interpretable. That’s why once the data is transformed into the integrated latent space, we don’t have actual count data anymore, and we can’t perform operations like differential expression analysis or other operations that require count data on this space. Yet, the latent space can be used as direct input for UMAP and t-SNE, and can improve clustering results thanks to the removal of batch effects.

## Dimensionality Reduction (continued)

### UMAP and t-SNE

UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) and t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) are non-linear dimensionality reduction techniques that help visualize the data by creating lower-dimensional representations of the data in 2D or 3D. They are particularly useful for visualizing clusters in single-cell RNA-seq data, as they can capture similarities and variation between cells visually.

To determine the dimensionality of the data, we will first plot an Elbow plot. We are trying to find the number of principal components that capture most of the variation in the data, forming the characteristic ‘elbow’ shape in the plot.

```{r tsne-umap}
ElbowPlot(aml)

## Run UMAP and t-SNE
aml <- RunUMAP(aml, dims = 1:30, verbose = FALSE)
aml <- RunTSNE(aml, dims = 1:30, verbose=FALSE)

## Plot results
DimPlot(aml, reduction = "umap", group.by = "Phase") + 
  ggtitle("UMAP")

DimPlot(aml, reduction = "tsne", group.by = "Phase") + ggtitle("t-SNE")

## Save the object
saveRDS(aml, file = file.path("results/sc-rnaseq/robj/aml.session2.RDS"))

## clear env
rm(list = ls())
gc()

```

# Clustering, differential gene expression analysis and functional analysis

Lets load the required libraries and RDS file from the previous section.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
suppressMessages(library(Seurat))
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))
suppressMessages(library(ggplot2))
suppressMessages(library(Seurat))
suppressMessages(library(enrichplot))
suppressMessages(library(pheatmap))
suppressMessages(library(viridis))
suppressMessages(library(scCustomize))
suppressMessages(library(ggalluvial))
suppressMessages(library(progeny))

## Load the saved object from previous session
aml <- readRDS("/home/rstudio/abptds/results/sc-rnaseq/robj/aml.session2.RDS")

```

## Clustering
Seurat applies a graph-based clustering approach. First, a KNN graph is constructed based on the euclidean distance in PCA space. For clustering, we apply the Louvain algorithm (`algorithm = 1`) which is the default modularity optimization method in Seurat. With the resolution parameter, it is possible to define the number of clusters.


Found clusters are visualized in UMAP visualization. Note that distance between clusters on the UMAP does not represent degree of similarity between clusters in the original data space. UMAP is a dimensionality reduction technique that prioritizes local structure preservation, meaning that while nearby points are generally more similar, global distances may not always be reliable for interpreting relationships between clusters.

```{r clustering}
## Find-k-nearest neighor
aml <- FindNeighbors(aml, dims = 1:30, reduction = "pca")

## Find clusters
aml <- FindClusters(aml, resolution = 0.5)

## UMAP 
DimPlot(aml, reduction = "umap", label= TRUE)

## can be visualized as PCA as well
DimPlot(aml,reduction="pca")
```

Let's inspect the Seurat object.

```{r}
head(aml@meta.data)

## get clusters
unique(aml@meta.data$seurat_clusters)

## using idents
unique(Idents(aml))

table(aml@meta.data$seurat_clusters)

```


Let's visualize the sample specificity of the clusters using a heatmap.

```{r}
## get cell numbers from each sample for seach cluster
df <- as.data.frame.matrix(table(aml$sample, aml$seurat_clusters))

## transpose
df <- t(df)

## convert to percentage
df <- df/rowSums(df)

## heatmap
pheatmap(t(df), display_numbers = TRUE)

```

An aluvial plot can also be useful when we want to visualizing sample specific cells assigned to the clusters.

```{r aluvial-plot}
## aluvial plot
plot.data <- aml@meta.data[,c("sample","seurat_clusters")]
colnames(plot.data) <- c("Samples", "Clusters")

## frequency per cluster
freq <- plot.data %>% 
  group_by(Samples,Clusters) %>% 
  summarize(count=n())


ggplot(as.data.frame(freq),
              aes(y = count, axis1 = Samples, axis2 = Clusters)) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(fill = Clusters), width = 1/12) +
  geom_stratum(width = 1/12, fill = "black", color = "grey") +
  geom_label(stat = "stratum", aes(label = after_stat(stratum))) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Slides", "Clusters"), expand = c(.05, .05)) 
```
We can use non numeric `aml@meta.data` columns to color a UMAP plot.

```{r}
## color by sample
DimPlot(aml, reduction = "umap", group.by = "sample")

## color by Phase
DimPlot(aml, reduction = "umap", group.by = "Phase")
```

## Differential Gene Expression (DGE) Analysis


Let's look for differentially expressed genes between the clusters. We use `FindMarkers` function that applies Wilcoxon Rank Sum test by default (`test.use = "wilcox"`) for differential testing. Differential testing is applied for normalized data which is found from `aml@assays$RNA$data`. 

Useful arguments in `FindMarkers` function are `min.pct` and `logfc.threshold`. By `min.pct`, you only test genes that are detected in a minimum fraction of `min.pct` cells in either of the two populations. By `logfc.threshold`, you can limit testing to genes which show, on average, at least X-fold difference (log-scale) between the two groups of cells. Default is 0.1 and the threshold speeds up the function, but can miss weaker signals.

First, we aim to identify all marker genes for cluster 0.

```{r dge-c8}
# one cluster versus all other
cluster0.markers <- FindMarkers(aml, ident.1 = 0, min.pct = 0.1, logfc.threshold = 0.1)
head(cluster0.markers)
```

FindMarkers function produces a data.frame with a ranked list of markers as rows and associated statistics as columns. It includes following columns: 

- `avg_logFC`: log fold-chage of the average expression between the two groups. Positive values indicate that the gene is more highly expressed in the first group.
- `pct.1`: The percentage of cells where the gene is detected in the first group.
- `pct.2`: The percentage of cells where the gene is detected in the second group.
- `p_val_adj`: Adjusted p-value based on bonferroni correction using all genes in the dataset.


Let's visualize the top DE genes for cluster 0 in a heatmap.

```{r top-markers-heatmap-1, warning=FALSE}
## get top 50 markers
top50 <- cluster0.markers %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var="gene") %>%
  top_n(n = 50, wt = avg_log2FC)

## plot
DoHeatmap(aml, features = top50$gene, size =3) + theme(text = element_text(size = 8)) + NoLegend()
```

We can also visualize the expression of top DE genes in violin and UMAP plots.

```{r top-DE-genes-visualization-1}
FeaturePlot(aml, features = c("IGLL1", "ITM2A", "TRH"))
VlnPlot(aml, features = c("IGLL1", "ITM2A", "TRH"), pt.size=0.1)
```


Next, we want to find markers for every cluster compared to all remaining cells. Here we check top 5 markers for every cluster based on log2FC.

```{r all-markers, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
all.markers <- FindAllMarkers(aml, min.pct = 0.1, logfc.threshold = 0.1)


all.markers %>%
    group_by(cluster) %>%
    slice_max(n = 5, order_by = avg_log2FC)
```

Here, we generate a heatmap showing the expression of the top 10 markers for each cluster.

```{r top-markers-heatmap-2, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
all.markers %>%
    group_by(cluster) %>%
    top_n(n = 10, wt = avg_log2FC) -> top10

DoHeatmap(aml, features = top10$gene, size = 3) + theme(text = element_text(size = 3)) + NoLegend() 
```

We can again visualize some markers. Let's take the top markers of the biggest cluster 0.

```{r top-DE-genes-visualization-2}
FeaturePlot(aml, features = c("IGLL1", "ITM2A", "TRH"))
VlnPlot(aml, features = c("IGLL1", "ITM2A", "TRH"), pt.size=0.1)
```


Based on the violin plot, we observe that the top markers for cluster 0 are also expressed in clusters 10 and 12, which are closely located on the UMAP. This suggests that the current clustering resolution may be too high, and these clusters could represent a single cell type. For the purpose of initial cell type annotation, we will retain the current resolution, although it is good to note that cell type annotation can be an iterative process, wherein optimal resolution is identified by refining the clustering and analyzing the biological relevance of the resulting groups 

For the visualization of marker expression, we can alternatively use a ridge plot. 

```{r top-DE-genes-alternative-visualization, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
RidgePlot(aml, features = c("IGLL1", "ITM2A", "TRH"), ncol =3)
```


If you wish more customization and visualization options for your single-cell RNA-seq analysis, there is the `scCustomize` package designed particularly for the output generated by Seurat (https://samuel-marsh.github.io/scCustomize/articles/Gene_Expression_Plotting.html). 

We can for example use custom color palettes which distinguish low expressing cells from non-expressing cells (non-expressing cells are part of same color scale in FeaturePlot function).

```{r sccustom-feature}
FeaturePlot_scCustom(aml, features = "TRH")

pal <- viridis(n = 10, option = "D")
FeaturePlot_scCustom(aml, features = "TRH", colors_use = pal)

```


We can also more easily visualize a marker expression in each sample separately.


```{r sccustom-density, fig.width=11, fig.height=8}
FeaturePlot_scCustom(aml, features = "CRYGD", split.by = "sample", num_columns = 2)
```

### Comparing two clusters

Sometimes, we are only interested in differences between specific clusters. To compare two clusters of interest, we use the `FindMarkers` function, specifying the cluster names in `ident.1` and `ident.2`. In this case, we compare clusters 2 and 4.

```{r dge-2}
# cluster2 versus cluster4
levels(aml)
c2.vs.c4.markers <- FindMarkers(aml, ident.1 = 2, ident.2 = 4, min.pct = 0.1, logfc.threshold = 0.1)

# first few lines of the result
head(c2.vs.c4.markers)
```

We want to plot only cells in these two clusters.

```{r subset-plotting}
# subsetting cells having identity 2 or 4
c2.c4.cells <- WhichCells(aml, idents=c("2", "4"))

# UMAP plot of cluster 9 and 10
UMAPPlot(aml, cells=c2.c4.cells, label.size=6, pt.size = 1)
```


Genes with a positive logFC are overexpressed in cluster 2, while those with a negative logFC are overexpressed in cluster 4. Here, we examine two of these differentially expressed genes.

```{r top-DE-genes-visualization-3, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
FeaturePlot_scCustom(aml, cells = c2.c4.cells, features = c("S100A9", "S100A8"))
```


### DGE between two sample groups

Next, we aim to determine whether we can identify differences in gene expression between disease stages by performing differential gene expression (DGE) analysis between diagnostic and refractory samples. To begin, we will create a new column in `meta.data` and set it as the identity class.

```{r DE-genes-2-samples}
aml@meta.data$stage[aml@meta.data$sample %in% c("AML1_D", "AML3_D")] <- "diagnosis"
aml@meta.data$stage[aml@meta.data$sample %in% c("AML2_R", "AML3_R")] <- "refractory"
Idents(aml) <- "stage"
levels(aml)

DimPlot(aml, reduction = "umap")

D.vs.R.markers <- FindMarkers(aml, ident.1 = "diagnosis",ident.2 = "refractory", min.pct = 0.1, logfc.threshold = 0.1)

head(D.vs.R.markers)
```
We again visualize the expression of a few marker genes. The results suggest that it is possible to identify genes that are specifically associated with either the diagnostic or refractory stage.

```{r top-DE-genes-visualization-4}
FeaturePlot_scCustom(aml,features = c("IGLL1","HERPUD1"), order = F)
VlnPlot(aml, features = c("IGLL1","HERPUD1"), pt.size=0.1)
```

## Functional analysis


### Gene Ontology GO over-representation analysis (ORA)

We perform over-representation analysis with ClusterProfiler. Over-representation analysis is a statistical method used to determine whether genes from predefined sets are present more frequently than expected in a given subset of the data. In this context, the subset refers to the set of upregulated or downregulated genes.

Tutorial for Over-representation analysis with ClusterProfiler: [https://yulab-smu.top/biomedical-knowledge-mining-book/clusterprofiler-go.html](https://yulab-smu.top/biomedical-knowledge-mining-book/clusterprofiler-go.html)

Here we define the annotation data set.

```{r annotation}
suppressMessages(library(clusterProfiler))

organism = "org.Hs.eg.db"
suppressMessages(library(organism, character.only = TRUE))
```

We are interested in biological annotation of cluster 0. We want to find biological process (BP) Gene Ontology terms that are enriched in cluster 0. First, we aim to filter the marker genes by selecting only those that are statistically significant after p-value adjustment and ensuring that they are truly representative of the cluster. If the gene set is too large, it may become too general, reducing the specificity of the analysis and potentially diluting meaningful biological insights.

```{r filt-c0}
cluster0.markers <- cluster0.markers[cluster0.markers$p_val_adj < 0.05,]
cluster0.markers <- cluster0.markers[cluster0.markers$pct.1 > 0.2,]
```

We aim to use the most upregulated genes of cluster 0 in ORA by selecting those that are expressed at least twice as much in cluster 0 cells compared to other cells. Here, we visualize the distribution of `avg_log2FC` values using a histogram to illustrate our selected threshold.


```{r filt-2-c0}
filt.markers <- cluster0.markers[cluster0.markers$avg_log2FC > 0.50,]
genes <- rownames(filt.markers)
length(genes)
```

## Creating enrichGO object

Gene ids are as "SYMBOL" and we use biological process (BP) as ontology. You can also try analysis with other ontologies: MF (Molecular Function) or CC (Cellular Component).

We have to define background genes first which we use as 'gene universe'. 

```{r enrich-c0}
gene.universe <- rownames(aml@assays$RNA)
c0.res <- enrichGO(gene = genes,
                      universe = gene.universe,
                      OrgDb = organism, 
                      keyType = 'SYMBOL',
                      readable = F,
                      ont = "BP",
                      pvalueCutoff = 0.05, 
                      qvalueCutoff = 0.01)

head(c0.res)
```

Let's visualize the results in a barplot.

```{r enrich-barplot-c0}
barplot(c0.res, 
        drop = TRUE, 
        showCategory = 10, 
        title = "Top GO terms (biological processes) in cluster 0",
        font.size = 8)

```

### Exercise 12

Perform Gene Ontology GO over-representation analysis using molecular function (`ont = "MF"`).


Finally, we save the `aml` object and clear the objects from the memory.

```{r}
## Save the object
saveRDS(aml, file = file.path("results/sc-rnaseq/robj/aml.session3.RDS"))

## clear env
rm(list = ls())
gc()
```

# Cell type annotation

## Manual annotation of cell types

Once the dataset is correctly preprocessed and batch effects are eliminated from the data, after performing dimensionality reduction, the cells from the same cell type tend to cluster together. We can use this property to manually check and annotate the clusters we have previously identified.


```{r manual-cell-type-annotation}
suppressMessages(library(Seurat))
suppressMessages(library(gridExtra))
suppressMessages(library(ggplot2))
suppressMessages(library(glmGamPoi))
suppressMessages(library(scCATCH))
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))

## load aml object
aml <- readRDS("/home/rstudio/abptds/results/sc-rnaseq/robj/aml.session3.RDS")

## UMAP
DimPlot(aml, reduction = "umap", group.by = "sample")

## Subset
aml2.r <- subset(aml, subset = sample=="AML2_R")

## Blast cells
FeaturePlot(aml2.r,features = c( "ANKRD28", "GNA15"))

## remove object
rm(aml2.r)
gc()

```



## Automatic cell-type annotation using markers (ScType)

There are some other problems with manual annotation:

- Time consuming
- Lower reproducibility
- Need of prior knowledge on the expected cell types
- Depend on a good cluster definition
- Identification of lower level or rare subtypes sometimes it's not possible

So let's take a look at other methods for cell annotation.
There are many annotation tools with different approaches and their performance might vary depending on the dataset (see review). Here, we will use [scCATCH](https://github.com/ZJUFanLab/scCATCH) for its simplicity.


```{r scCatch}
# extract normalized count and cluster info from Seurat object
mat <- aml@assays$RNA$data
clust    <- as.character( aml@meta.data$seurat_clusters )


## create scCATCH obj
sc.catch.obj <- createscCATCH(data = mat, cluster = clust)

## find markers
sc.catch.obj <- findmarkergene(sc.catch.obj, species="Human", marker=cellmatch, tissue=c("Bone marrow"))

## find cell type for each cluster
sc.catch.obj <- findcelltype(sc.catch.obj)

## list cell types
celltype.pred <- sc.catch.obj@celltype

## remove obj
rm(sc.catch.obj)
gc()
```

Now, lets apply the detected cell types information in Seurat object `aml`.

```{r apply-cell-types}

DimPlot(aml, reduction = "umap", group.by = "seurat_clusters", label = TRUE)

new.cell.ids <-  aml@meta.data$seurat_clusters 


new.cell.ids <- gsub("^2$", "Stromal Cell", new.cell.ids)
new.cell.ids <- gsub(4, "Monocyte, Stem Cell", new.cell.ids)
new.cell.ids <- gsub(5, "Mesenchymal Stem Cell", new.cell.ids)
new.cell.ids <- gsub(7, "Macrophage", new.cell.ids)
new.cell.ids <- gsub(8, "Mesenchymal Stromal Cell", new.cell.ids)

aml <-AddMetaData(aml, new.cell.ids, col.name="cell_type")
DimPlot(aml, reduction = "umap", label = TRUE, pt.size = 0.5, group.by = "cell_type", repel = TRUE) + NoLegend()


## clear env totally
rm(list = ls())
gc()

```

# A complete workflow

Here is a summary of a complete analysis workflow.

## Loading the data

Firstly, we have to load the data. In the following code block we are using the aggregate data.

```{r wrkflow-data-loading, warning=FALSE}

## read 10X data
aml <- Read10X(data.dir = file.path("/home/rstudio/abptds/data/sc-rnaseq/aggregate"))

## create a seurat object
aml.all <- CreateSeuratObject(counts=aml, names.delim = "-", names.field = 2)

## set new identities
aml.all <- RenameIdents(aml.all, '1' = "AML2_R", "2" = "AML1_D", "3"="AML3_D", "4"="AML3_R")
table( Idents(aml.all) )

## add 'sample' column to aml.all@meta.data dataframe
aml.all <- AddMetaData(aml.all, Idents(aml.all), col.name = "sample")

## Calculate MT genes
aml.all[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(aml.all, pattern = "^MT-")

## Calculate globin genes
aml.all[["percent.globin"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(aml.all, pattern = "HBA1| HBA-Z | HBE | HBG1 | HBG12 | HBD | HBB | MB")
```


## QC-plots

The second step is to check QC. Please note that , in the above code block we have calculated `percent.globin`.

```{r wrkflow-qc, warning=FALSE}
## violin plot showing nFeature_RNA, nCount_RNA and percent.mt
VlnPlot(aml.all, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"))

## globin %
VlnPlot(aml.all, features = c("percent.globin"))

## scatter plot nCount_RNA vs. percent.mt
FeatureScatter(aml.all, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "percent.mt") +
           theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust=1)) 

## scatter plot nCount_RNA vs. nFeature_RNA
FeatureScatter(aml.all, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "nFeature_RNA") +
   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust=1))
```

## Filtering

Based on above QC plots, we are filtering cells based on `nFeature_RNA`, `nFeature_RNA`, `percent.mt`, and `percent.globin`.

```{r wrkflow-filt, warning=FALSE}
## Filter
temp1 <- subset(aml.all, subset = nFeature_RNA > 500 & nFeature_RNA < 3500 & percent.mt < 10 & percent.globin < 2 & sample=="AML1_D")
temp2 <- subset(aml.all, subset = nFeature_RNA > 500 & nFeature_RNA < 3000 & percent.mt < 10 & percent.globin < 2 & sample=="AML2_R")
temp3 <- subset(aml.all, subset = nFeature_RNA > 500 & nFeature_RNA < 2500 & percent.mt < 10 & percent.globin < 2 & sample=="AML3_D")
temp4 <- subset(aml.all, subset = nFeature_RNA > 600 & nFeature_RNA < 3000 & percent.mt < 10 & percent.globin < 2 & sample=="AML3_R")

## create a new aggregated data object
aml.filt <- merge(temp1,  list(temp2, temp3, temp4))
aml.filt <- JoinLayers(aml.filt)

## violin plot showing nFeature_RNA, nCount_RNA and percent.mt
VlnPlot(aml.filt, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"))

## scatter plot nCount_RNA vs. percent.mt
FeatureScatter(aml.filt, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "percent.mt") +
           theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust=1)) 

## scatter plot nCount_RNA vs. nFeature_RNA
FeatureScatter(aml.filt, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "nFeature_RNA") +
   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust=1))

## remov eobjects
rm(temp1, temp2, temp3, temp4)
gc()
```

## Normalization and Variable features detection

After filtering, we are normalizing the data and calculating highly variable genes.

```{r wrkflow-norm, warning=FALSE}
## normalization
aml.filt <- NormalizeData(aml.filt)

## calculate variable features
aml.filt <- FindVariableFeatures(aml.filt, nfeatures=2000, verbose = FALSE)

## Get top 10 most highly variable genes
top10 <- head(VariableFeatures(aml.filt), 10)
top10

## Plot HVGs with labels
hvg <- VariableFeaturePlot(aml.filt) + labs(title = 'HVGs')
LabelPoints(plot = hvg, points = top10, repel = TRUE) + labs(title = 'HVGs, top10 HVGs labeled')
```
## Scaling the data, the removal of undesired sources of variation

Next step is to scale the data. In the following block we are regressing out the variables `percent.mt`, `percent.globin`, `S.Score`, `G2M.Score` on the same go.

```{r wrkflow-scale, warning=FALSE}
## cell cycle scoring
aml.filt <- CellCycleScoring(aml.filt,
                        s.features = cc.genes$s.genes,
                        g2m.features = cc.genes$g2m.genes,
                        set.ident = TRUE)

## scaling and regressing-out undesired variance
aml.filt <- ScaleData(aml.filt,
                 vars.to.regress = c("percent.mt", "percent.globin", "S.Score", "G2M.Score"),
                 layer = "data",
                 verbose = FALSE)

```
## Dimensionality reduction

After adjusting all the possible biases, we perform the dimensional reduction and clustering.

```{r wrkflow-dim}
## Run PCA
aml.filt <- RunPCA(aml.filt,
              features = VariableFeatures(aml.filt),
              ndims.print = 1:3,
              nfeatures.print = 20)


## Visualize PCA results
DimPlot(aml.filt,
        reduction = "pca",
        group.by = "sample")

## PCA heatmap
DimHeatmap(aml.filt, dims = 1:6, cells = 500, balanced = TRUE, fast = FALSE)
DimHeatmap(aml.filt, dims = 7:12, cells = 500, balanced = TRUE, fast = FALSE)

# Elbow plot
ElbowPlot(aml.filt, ndims = 50)

## Run UMAP
aml.filt <- RunUMAP(aml.filt, dims = 1:30, verbose = FALSE)

## Run clustering
## Find-k-nearest neighbor
aml.filt <- FindNeighbors(aml.filt, dims = 1:30, reduction = "pca")

## Find clusters
aml.filt <- FindClusters(aml.filt)

## UMAP 
DimPlot(aml.filt, reduction = "umap", label= TRUE)
DimPlot(aml.filt, reduction = "umap", label= TRUE, group.by = "sample")
```

## Differential gene expression

From the above code block we have got clusters. Now, we want to find markers of those clusters.

```{r wrkflow-dge, warning=FALSE}
## get all markers
all.markers  <- FindAllMarkers(aml.filt, min.pct = 0.1, logfc.threshold = 0.25)

## filter markers
markers.filt <- all.markers[all.markers$p_val_adj < 0.05,]

## top 10 per cluster
markers.filt %>%
    group_by(cluster) %>%
    top_n(n = 10, wt = avg_log2FC) -> top10

DoHeatmap(aml.filt, features = top10$gene, size = 3) + theme(text = element_text(size = 3)) + NoLegend() 

```

## Cell type annotation

In the following code block we are using scCATCH to detect cell types automatically.

```{r wrkflow-cell-type}
## create scCATCH obj
sc.catch <- createscCATCH(data = aml.filt@assays$RNA$data, cluster = as.character( aml.filt@meta.data$seurat_clusters ) )

## find markers
sc.catch <- findmarkergene(sc.catch, species="Human", marker=cellmatch, tissue=c("Bone marrow"))

## find cell type for each cluster
sc.catch <- findcelltype(sc.catch)

## list cell types
cell.type.pred <- sc.catch@celltype

## show the predicted cell types
cell.type.pred

## remove obj
rm(sc.catch)
gc()
```
